title: Choosing her own material, 'Mad About the Boy' and getting tired of folk songs
summary: She selected the songs herself, wanted to stretch out, and was tired of being identified with folk-song swing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: I noticed you also included in that selection a Noel Coward song.
Yes.
'Mad About The Boy.'
Yes.
From what I remember, that's probably the most experimental arrangement of the whole thing.

I would think so too, yes. I selected that -- I selected all of these things because they wanted to know what did I want to do. Of course, they made the arrangements. 'I Must Have That Man' -- I think that's another one that I had remembered that Adelaide Hall had done in the (inaudible). And I always wanted to do 'I Can't Get Started

With You." These were songs -- a lot of the -- if you want to call them the standards -- these had been things that I had been doing in the clubs, and not necessarily having recorded them in the past. Because the recording weren't interested in my doing these type of things. They were only interested in me trying to find as many "Loch Lomond's" as I could.
Yes.
But this was a chance for me to stretch out a little bit.
Did it make a difference to you to have the opportunity to select your own material?
Yes!
Was it a very important consideration --
Yes! Because I felt -- Well, first of all, I got tired of being identified with "Loch Lomond" and these folk things. And then -- although I started doing some

of these things long before the folk craze got popular -- by the time after a few years, then you had the real folk singers doing the real folk songs, and it made it looked like I was doing camp, or something like that.
So, I had to find, you know, something else to do. And, of course, I had always wanted to do the standard pop thing in a little freer than I had been doing.
Because I felt that I was being held back from the beginning, you know -- from the very first day. He said, you know, "Don't because you're going to sound like Ella Fitzgerald or somebody else."
But at this particular point, it didn't matter. I mean I was already established.

And this didn't make much difference. I mean, I made the records -- maybe somebody bought them for what they were worth -- but the real -- some of the best things that I feel that I made were the next group of things I made with Ellis Larkin.
Yeah.
I really felt very good
